speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to your appointment. As a newborn, your condition is urgent; I need to know how many days old you are and if you have had any fever, difficulty breathing, or poor feeding. REQUEST TEST: Complete blood count, C-Reactive protein, and Blood glucose.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for the normal initial lab results. Given your age and the need to rule out serious infections or metabolic issues, do you notice if you have been passing stool or urine since birth?

speaker: Patient
text: Newborn, female. The patient is a 3000-g (6.6-lb) female newborn delivered at term to a 23-year-old primigravida mother. The mother reports having had no prenatal care, and immunization records for the newborn are not available.

speaker: Doctor
text: Good morning. I see you are a term female newborn with a mother who had no prenatal care; based on this, I must ask if you have experienced jaundice, poor feeding, or a fever. REQUEST TEST: Bilirubin level, Blood glucose, and Gram stain from any open umbilical cord sites. REQUEST IMAGES: Physical examination photos focusing on the skin, abdomen, and umbilical region.

speaker: Doctor
text: The initial labs were normal. Given your mother's lack of prenatal care, I need to know if you are passing stool and urine, and if you have any visible jaundice or a red, foul-smelling umbilical cord. REQUEST TEST: Total bilirubin level.

speaker: Doctor
text: Thank you for confirming normal readings. Given the lack of prenatal care, have you observed any yellow discoloration of the skin, or is the umbilical cord red, swollen, or foul-smelling?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Continuous heart murmur. I also have Bluish macules on the skin that do not blanch with pressure, Cloudy lenses in both eyes noticed upon examination, Failure to pass auditory screening tests.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: DiGeorge Syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome).

The combination of a continuous heart murmur (suggesting patent ductus arteriosus), bluish macules (nevus of Ota/blue rubber bleb nevus), and cataracts (blue dot cataracts) in a newborn with no prenatal care is highly characteristic of DiGeorge Syndrome. I am ready to confirm this with genetic testing.
